opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we're still in the very early days here, and a lot of what's been done so far is fairly blunt. The first generation of interventions was things like reinforcement learning from human feedback, content filters, and system prompts telling the model what not to say. Those help, but they're coarse. You often end up with a model that's either overly cautious and refuses perfectly reasonable requests, or one that can be talked out of its guardrails with a clever enough prompt.

Where I'd like to see things go, and this connects to the algorithmic fairness work I've been involved with for years, is toward being much more precise about what we actually mean. "Toxicity" and "trustworthiness" aren't single numbers. They're contextual and multidimensional, and they vary across communities and use cases. A lot of progress in fairness came when people stopped saying "the algorithm should be fair" and started writing down specific definitions, then studying the trade-offs between them and against accuracy. I think we need the same discipline here. What exactly are we constraining, how do we measure it, and what are we giving up to get it?

The second thing is that I'd like interventions to move from being bolted on after the fact to being more principled and auditable. Right now, if you ask why a model refused something, or why it cited one source and not another, there often isn't a satisfying answer. If we want these systems to steer people toward trusted information, there needs to be some transparency about what counts as trusted and who decided. Otherwise you've just moved the editorial judgment somewhere opaque.

Related to that, I think external auditing and evaluation will become increasingly important. You can't rely entirely on the developers to grade their own homework. We need good tools, ideally ones that work with limited access to the model, so that third parties, regulators, or researchers can probe whether a model behaves the way its builders claim, across different populations and different kinds of queries.

Finally, I'd stress humility about the trade-offs. Every intervention that pushes a model away from one kind of harm can introduce another, whether that's erasing legitimate minority viewpoints, being paternalistic, or just being less useful. Those aren't reasons not to intervene. They're reasons to be explicit about the choices, measure them, and let society weigh in, rather than pretending there's a technical fix that makes the hard normative questions go away.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses blunt interventions such as RLHF, filters, and system prompts, and calls for more precise, auditable interventions. It does not clearly advocate incorporating their behavioral objectives into the model training process itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the current approaches are still pretty blunt instruments. Most of what we do today happens either at pretraining time, where you're curating or filtering the data, or at the fine-tuning and RLHF stage, where you're essentially nudging the model's behavior with human preference signals. Both of those are useful, but they have a kind of monolithic quality to them. You're trying to bake one notion of "trusted" and one notion of "toxic" into a single model that's going to be deployed to an enormous and diverse population of users, in contexts you can't fully anticipate.

So where I'd like to see things evolve is toward interventions that are more modular, more targeted, and frankly more accountable. Let me unpack that a little.

By modular, I mean separating the capability of the model from the policy about what it should and shouldn't say. Right now those are entangled. If I want to change the model's behavior around, say, medical misinformation, I'm often retraining or re-fine-tuning something enormous, and I have limited ability to verify that I haven't changed other things in the process. Techniques like retrieval augmentation, where the model is pointed at a curated corpus for factual grounding, or steering at inference time rather than training time, give you something closer to a dial you can adjust and audit, instead of a black box you re-bake.

By targeted, I mean we need to get much more precise about what we're actually optimizing for. "Toxicity" is not one thing. "Trusted information" is not one thing, and I'd argue it's even more fraught, because who decides what's trusted is a genuinely contested question. I come at this partly from the algorithmic fairness world, and one lesson there is that when you reduce a rich normative concept to a single scalar and optimize it, you often get something that satisfies the metric and violates the intent. I worry about the same thing with toxicity classifiers and trust scores. So I'd like to see interventions that are specified in terms of concrete, checkable constraints, and ideally that different deployers or even different users can set differently within some outer bounds.

And by accountable, I mean we should be able to say, after the fact, what intervention was applied, what it was designed to do, and whether it did it. There's a lot of interesting work right now on things like interpretability and on provable or at least measurable guarantees about model behavior. I'm not naive about how far that's gotten, but I think the direction is right. If you tell me a model has been steered away from toxicity, I want to know what that means operationally, on what distribution of inputs, and what the failure rate is. That's the kind of thing we insist on in other domains where algorithms make consequential decisions, and I don't see why language models should be exempt.

The last thing I'd say is that I think we should be a bit humble about the limits of technical interventions here. Some of what we're asking these systems to do, like arbitrate what information is trustworthy, is really a social and institutional problem that we're trying to offload onto a model. The technical work matters, but the thing I'd push hardest on is being explicit about the values and tradeoffs being encoded, rather than letting them live implicitly inside a reward model somewhere.

r001.rationale: The response describes pretraining and fine-tuning as current approaches, but advocates modular interventions such as retrieval augmentation and inference-time steering. It does not advocate incorporating post hoc intervention objectives into model training itself.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to move from treating these interventions as one-time fixes to treating them as an ongoing process. You can fine-tune a model to prefer reliable sources or avoid certain kinds of toxic responses, but that doesn’t give you a guarantee about how it will behave in every new context.

And these are distinct problems. A response can be perfectly polite and completely wrong. So we need to be explicit about what we’re trying to improve, how we measure it, and what tradeoffs an intervention introduces. Are we reducing harmful responses while also making the model refuse legitimate questions? Are we encouraging trusted information, or just teaching the model to sound authoritative?

I’d like to see interventions become more targeted and more measurable, with evaluation continuing after deployment. For factual questions, that might mean grounding answers in sources that can actually be checked and allowing the system to express uncertainty. For toxicity, it means paying attention to context rather than simply filtering words. The broader point is that steering the model is an engineering tool; it isn’t, by itself, evidence that we’ve solved the underlying problem.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fine-tuning for reliability or toxicity, but does not advocate incorporating objectives from post hoc interventions into the model’s training process itself. It emphasizes ongoing, targeted interventions and evaluation after deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they have to evolve beyond the idea that there’s one intervention that will solve the problem. You can curate the training data, you can fine-tune the model, you can put filters on its outputs, and you can have it retrieve information from sources you trust. Each of those helps in particular ways, but each also has limitations.

And we need to be precise about what we’re trying to accomplish. Producing factually reliable answers and avoiding toxic language are different objectives. A model can be perfectly polite and completely wrong. So we need evaluations that distinguish those things and look at how the system behaves in context, including when somebody is actively trying to defeat the safeguards.

I’d like to see these systems become better at communicating the basis for an answer and recognizing when they don’t have enough evidence. Connecting a model to trusted information is useful, but it doesn’t automatically mean the model will use that information faithfully. That’s something you have to measure. The broader direction should be toward interventions whose effects we can characterize, whose tradeoffs we understand, and that we can keep adapting as the models and their uses change.

r001.rationale: The response lists fine-tuning as one possible intervention, but does not advocate incorporating the behavioral objectives enforced by post hoc interventions into the model’s training process itself.
